original_question: Strengthen the invariant theory for long virtual knots and long flat virtual knots, especially by combining the long-knot approach of [160] with biquandle constructions, by extracting useful classical-knot invariants from that framework, and by seeking a full classification of long flat knots using the descending-diagram construction D(F) associated to a long flat virtual knot F.
target_in_paper: Section 8.1, Problem 7 (“Long knots and long flat knots”).
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the exact cluster of questions posed in Section 8.1, Problem 7: enlarging the long-knot invariant structure from Manturov’s work, combining it with biquandle methods, asking whether this yields new classical-knot invariants, and using Turaev’s descending-diagram construction D(F) for long flat virtual knots. It also correctly recognizes that the paper treats D(F) as a way to pull virtual-knot invariants back to long flat virtual knots and connects this to classification.
missing_details: The cited long-knot source in the paper is reference [167], not [160]. The paper names it as V. O. Manturov, Long virtual knots and their invariants.
The objects are specifically long virtual knots and long flat virtual knots; the paper’s shorthand “long flat knots” means long flat virtual knots in this context.
The paper’s background context defines long knots as 1-1 tangles obtained by breaking a knot and sending the ends to infinity along a horizontal axis.

The paper does not ask for a general ‘strengthening of invariant theory’; it asks more narrowly to enlarge the long-knot invariant structure of [167] and to obtain more powerful invariants of long knots.
The classical-knot part is phrased specifically as: ‘Can one get new classical knot invariants from the approach in this paper?’

The D(F) construction must be stated precisely: for a given long flat virtual knot diagram F, D(F) is the descending long virtual diagram obtained by resolving each flat non-virtual crossing so that one always goes over before going under.
What is invariant is the long virtual knot type of D(F), not merely the chosen diagram.
The universal pullback statement should be made explicit: for any virtual-knot invariant I, the quantity I[D(F)] is an invariant of the long flat virtual knot F.
The paper explicitly mentions doing sample calculations of such induced invariants; your draft omits this concrete intermediate task.

Your final clause about ‘seeking a full classification’ matches Section 8.1, Problem 7, but later in the same paper Section 8.4 says that long flat virtual knots can in fact be completely classified via signed permutations and are equivalent to long descending virtual knots. So, as a whole-paper reading, that part of your draft needs qualification.
refined_question: In the setting of long virtual knots (equivalently, 1-1 tangles) and long flat virtual knots, can one enlarge the long-knot invariant structure of Manturov [167] by combining it with the biquandle construction of Kauffman–Radford [130] to obtain stronger invariants of long virtual knots, and in particular to extract new classical-knot invariants from that framework? More concretely, if F is a long flat virtual knot diagram and D(F) denotes the descending long virtual knot obtained by resolving each flat non-virtual crossing so that one always passes over before under, then since the long virtual knot type of D(F) is an invariant of F, determine which virtual-knot invariants I make I(D(F)) into effective invariants of long flat virtual knots, carry out sample calculations of such induced invariants, and assess whether this descending-diagram method yields a classification of long flat virtual knots in the sense posed in Section 8.1.
justification: The draft is aiming almost verbatim at Section 8.1, Problem 7. The paper first sets the long-knot context in Section 2.3 by explaining long knots as 1-1 tangles and emphasizing that long virtual knots behave differently from compact virtual knots. Problem 7 then asks to enlarge Manturov’s long-knot invariant structure [167], asks whether that approach yields new classical-knot invariants, proposes combining it with the biquandle construction [130], and introduces Turaev’s descending-diagram map F -> D(F) for long flat virtual knot diagrams. The problem explicitly states that the long virtual knot type of D(F) is an invariant of F, so any virtual-knot invariant I gives an invariant I[D(F)] of the long flat knot F, and it explicitly mentions both sample calculations and the deeper classification problem. However, the later discussion in Section 8.4 qualifies the last point by stating that long flat virtual knots can be completely classified via a signed-permutation model and are equivalent to long descending virtual knots; thus your draft is faithful to the local Problem 7 formulation, but not to the paper’s later global update on the classification issue.
